title: Legal settlement discussions
scenario: A company is defending a lawsuit. Outside counsel initially believes the company will probably prevail.

timeline.event: Outside counsel says the company will probably prevail.
Plaintiff offers to settle for $20 million. The company rejects the offer.
Company counsel recommends offering $12 million.
The company offers $12 million.
Plaintiff counters at $15 million.
The parties agree in principle to settle for $14 million.
The settlement agreement is signed.
The company pays $14 million.

question: Which event most clearly establishes the accounting trigger for recognizing the settlement obligation?
answers: Apr 15 — the plaintiff first offers to settle
May 10 — the company makes its first offer
May 20 — the parties agree in principle on $14 million
Jun 5 — the formal agreement is signed
explanation: The key is when available evidence supports that a loss is probable and reasonably estimable. Agreement in principle is a strong recognition point; signing and payment are later legal/settlement events.

title: Warehouse fire
scenario: A fire severely damages a distribution center. The property is insured.

timeline.event: The fire occurs and severely damages the building.
Management estimates the property loss at $8 million.
The insurer confirms that the event is covered.
The insurer agrees to pay $7 million.
The insurance proceeds are received.

question: What is the first event that triggers recognition of the property loss?
answers: Feb 10 — the insurer agrees to pay
explanation: The casualty event causes the asset loss. Measurement may be refined afterward. The insurance recovery is a separate accounting analysis.

title: Demand collapse
scenario: A company carries $40 million of inventory for a product whose market changes abruptly.

timeline.event: Sales slow by 10%.
A competitor launches a substantially better product.
Market prices for the company's product fall 40%.
Management decides to discontinue the product.
The remaining inventory is sold at a substantial loss.

question: Which event most clearly triggers a reassessment of inventory carrying value?
answers: Q2 — competitor launches a better product
explanation: A sharp market-price decline is direct evidence that carrying value may no longer be recoverable. The later sale merely realizes the economics already evident earlier.

title: Loss of a major customer
scenario: A customer represents 28% of annual sales and is critical to one reporting unit.

timeline.event: The customer complains about pricing.
The customer begins a competitive bid process.
Management concludes the customer will probably leave.
The customer formally terminates the relationship.
Revenue from the customer ends.

question: Which event most clearly triggers an impairment assessment?
answers: Oct 20 — management concludes departure is probable
explanation: The accounting question begins when facts indicate that asset recoverability or fair value may have changed materially. Recognition of an impairment, however, requires the applicable impairment test.

title: Employee termination
scenario: Management develops and approves a one-time involuntary termination plan affecting 75 employees.

timeline.event: Management begins discussing reductions.
Management approves a detailed plan.
Affected employees are notified and the offer cannot realistically be withdrawn.
Employees stop working.
Severance is paid.

question: Which event is the best recognition trigger for the one-time termination benefits in this scenario?
answers: Jan 25 — employees are notified and the offer is effectively irrevocable
explanation: For one-time involuntary termination benefits, recognition generally depends on communication of a sufficiently detailed plan and satisfaction of the applicable criteria—not merely an internal decision.

title: Exit from a building
scenario: The company decides to permanently leave a leased office but continues to use it during a four-month transition.

timeline.event: Management decides to exit the office.
The board approves the restructuring plan.
Employees are told the office will close.
Operations cease and the facility is fully vacated.
The landlord takes possession.

question: Which event is most directly associated with complete cessation of use?
answers: May 31 — operations cease and the site is vacated
explanation: The decision to exit may itself be an impairment indicator, while complete cessation of use occurs when the company actually stops using and vacates the site. Different accounting consequences can therefore have different triggers.

title: Adverse court judgment
scenario: A company is defending a material lawsuit and had previously concluded that loss was not probable.

timeline.event: Trial begins.
Outside counsel says the case has become more difficult but still believes loss is not probable.
The court issues an adverse $25 million judgment.
The company announces that it will appeal.
The appeal is filed.

question: Which event most clearly requires the company to reassess its loss contingency conclusion?
explanation: An adverse judgment is significant new evidence and requires an immediate reassessment of probability, measurement, and disclosure even if the company intends to appeal.

title: Customer bankruptcy after year-end
scenario: A major customer owes $9 million at December 31. The financial statements have not yet been issued.

timeline.event: Receivable balance is $9 million and customer is paying slowly.
Customer misses another scheduled payment.
Customer files for bankruptcy.
Company estimates recovery of only $2 million.
Financial statements are issued.

question: Which event provides the strongest evidence about conditions that may have existed at year-end?
explanation: A bankruptcy shortly after year-end can provide evidence about the customer's financial condition at the balance-sheet date, making it a classic subsequent-event judgment.
